newsitem.title: USA: Dole likens himself to "plainspoken" Truman, Ike.
newsitem.headline: Dole likens himself to "plainspoken" Truman, Ike.

text.p: Likening himself to "plain-spoken" and honest Presidents Harry Truman and Dwight Eisenhower, Republican Bob Dole predicted on Friday Americans would decide on Election Day he was the only man they trusted to be their leader.
Campaigning by bus through Ohio for the second day, Dole once again drew comparisons between himself as trustworthy and President Bill Clinton as a promise breaker.

"I'm a plain-spoken man. I'm sort of like Harry Truman and Ike Eisenhower and others that you're aware of," the former Kansas senator said. "We're not as articulate or whatever, but we like to tell the truth, and we feel bad if we don't tell the truth," he said.

"We feel bad if we look you in the eye and say we're going to cut your taxes and then we raise your taxes," he said, reminding the crowd at the University of Findlay of Clinton's 1992 pledge to cut middle-class taxes.
Truman was a Democrat and Eisenhower a Republican but they both represent the nostalgic images that Dole, 73, often evokes of a happier and safer mid-century America.

At another rally in Lima, he predicted that on Nov. 5 people would enter voting booths and ask themselves, "Which one of these men ... can I trust? And they're going to say Bob Dole, Bob Dole, Bob Dole."
Campaigning as a "man of honour," Dole managed to press the issue of trust without directly wading into the "character issue" that some fellow Republicans have urged him to take on.

"They (American voters) knew all along about the continuing series of scandals that has plagued the Clinton administration for four year," campaign spokesman Nelson Warfield said. "It's in the public psyche."

One of the Republicans who has urged a more aggressive stance, former Education Secretary Bill Bennett, campaigned alongside Dole on Friday and described him at a rally in Lima as "a man whose word is his bond, that is, a man who believes in the old fashioned virtues, honour and honesty."

Dole has indicated repeatedly he does not want to start mudslinging. But each time he does not take the bait when invited to attack Clinton, the character issue gets raised in the media without Dole risking being portrayed as a villain.

Although new public opinion surveys show Dole still lagging Clinton, and some polls show a gap still in the double digits, Warfield said the campaign had always forecast that the race would narrow as election day approached.
"It's probably going to keep the other guys up at night," Warfield said.

A CNN/Gallup tracking poll showed the race tightening to 12 percentage points from 21 points mid-week. A tracking poll by the Political Hotline newsletter showed the race narrowed slightly to 15 points.

The Reuters tracking poll put the difference between Clinton and Dole at 9.7 percentage points on Friday. A Field poll in the largest electoral prize, California, showed Dole trailing by 10 points in that state, down from recent surveys.
Ohio, which has 21 electoral votes, chose Clinton in 1992 and polls show he is ahead in the state again. But a victory in Ohio is crucial to Dole this year.

Dole has seemed to enjoy himself on this trip, stopping at a small town bakery that boasts it makes the world's biggest pumpkin pie, standing in the shadow of grain silos or bathed in the light of the ferris wheel at a county fair and telling jokes over the microphone.
